title: AI in Legal Education: Law School Policy Archive
pub: Suffolk University Law School (personal project site of Dean Andrew Perlman)
author: Andrew Perlman

dom.t: School policies: Coverage maps do not measure strength

st.t: AI curriculum: Assistance must preserve intellectual development
st.an: The archive accepts the cluster’s practical balance by documenting curricula that combine supervised AI use with unaided foundational work, verification and preserved professional judgment. It materially extends the synthesis through a structured inventory distinguishing practical training from AI-law instruction, study from assessed work, and operative rules from guidance or future plans, while cautioning that these activities do not establish learning gains or national adoption rates.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The archive materially develops the cluster’s distinction between AI exposure and professional readiness by separating private study, assessed work, examinations and skills instruction, and by documenting layered models that preserve unaided foundations while introducing supervised AI use. Its evidence is descriptive, however, and does not establish durable competence or learning outcomes.
qs: ### AI use for studying and learning (`student-use`) — 42 schools  **Topic definition (workbook text):** School-level rules or guidance about using AI for private, non-submitted study—for example, preparing outlines, reviewing case holdings or arguments, clarifying concepts, practicing, or using study materials.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The archive extends the cluster’s selective-deployment and operating-model thesis into legal education. It documents use-specific controls, screening requirements and concrete assessment redesign rather than treating AI as uniformly permitted or prohibited.
qs: Course content, presentation notes, and unpublished research must be screened and may be uploaded only after verifying that they contain no information barred from upload.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: The archive supports the synthesis by documenting differentiated policies that combine staged or supervised AI instruction with restrictions on submitted work and assessments. Its category-based inventory is descriptive and does not treat institutional adoption counts as evidence of educational effectiveness or endorse a uniform timing rule.

st.t: Law-school policy: Staged use bridges bans and adoption
st.an: The archive supports the cluster’s staged-use proposition descriptively: it documents policies that protect unaided or independently assessed work while permitting supervised AI learning and professional training. Its strongest example is Chicago’s layered first-year pilot. However, the archive does not endorse that model or establish its educational effectiveness.
qs: What schools are doing:** The catalogued approaches generally allow limited non-submitted study support while preserving independent judgment and accuracy checks.

st.t: School policies: Coverage maps do not measure strength
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s descriptive proposition: it inventories 163 catalogued schools, reports varying topic counts, and distinguishes policy-status labels. It offers no substantive policy provisions, outcome evidence, or educational recommendation from which policy strength or preferred educational approaches could be inferred.

kp.k: Inventory documents varied educational responses, not national adoption rates
kp.d: The archive reports 163 U.S. law schools and 524 school-topic records across nine topics, with research last updated August 8, 2026. It is comparative, non-ranking and source-driven; its roster was cross-checked against the ABA Council list, but it does not claim exhaustive review. The appended tabulations describe archive contents rather than the population of U.S. law schools, and omission cannot establish absence of policy or practice.
qs: Workbook scope | 163 U.S. law schools | Site-aligned topic definitions, summaries, evidence labels, and source links.
School-topic records | 524
This remains a source-driven inventory rather than a claim that every approved school has been exhaustively reviewed or has a public AI policy or strategy.
They describe the archive's contents, not the population of US law schools

kp.k: Extensive AI-assisted compilation limits independent verification
kp.d: The archive discloses that ChatGPT Sites located sources, categorized records and helped draft and update summaries. Andrew Perlman did not manually review or independently confirm every reference or summary. Although the archive reports checking linked materials against summaries and categories at the August 8 update, it acknowledges possible errors, stale links and omissions. The school-specific evidence here is therefore the archive's reporting of linked materials, not independent confirmation of each underlying policy.
qs: ChatGPT Sites was used extensively to research and build this archive.
Andrew Perlman has not manually reviewed or independently confirmed every reference or every summary on the site.
Errors, stale links, and omissions may remain.

kp.k: Policy records must be distinguished from guidance and plans
kp.d: The archive separates operative policies, nonbinding guidance, interim measures, pilots, future adopted requirements, tentative schedules and completed offerings. The supplied derived distribution includes 314 records labeled In effect, 151 Guidance and 18 Completed/limited, alongside other and combined labels. These are school-topic record counts, not counts of distinct schools adopting binding policies. Universitywide policy inclusion is conditional on documented applicability to the law school.
qs: Each record is labeled as policy, guidance, or support rather than treating those categories as interchangeable.
| In effect | 314 |
| Guidance | 151 |
| Completed/limited | 18 |
No professional-school exclusion may appear.

kp.k: No single national law-school AI policy model governs
kp.d: The archive states that no public ABA legal-education rule or AALS classroom rule prescribes a uniform AI policy. It reports ABA recognition of widespread adaptation and AALS programming supporting responses. Institutional variation therefore remains central to the records, rather than compliance with a single national classroom model.
qs: No public ABA legal-education rule or AALS classroom rule prescribes a single law-school AI policy model.
The ABA has reported widespread policy adaptation, while AALS programming has focused on helping schools and faculty respond to AI.

kp.k: Private study permissions preserve independent judgment and verification
kp.d: The archive catalogs private-study rules or guidance for 42 schools. Its synthesis describes generally limited permission, often subordinate to course instructions. Examples include conceptual explanations, outlines, practice questions and brainstorming. Harvard distinguishes permissible exam preparation from pre-writing text for later exam answers; Kansas frames AI as supplemental rather than a substitute for students' thinking.
qs: The catalogued approaches generally allow limited non-submitted study support while preserving independent judgment and accuracy checks.

The 2025–26 Handbook of Academic Policies expressly permits students to prompt AI while studying for an exam about relevant topics or concepts, but not to have AI pre-write text that the student later incorporates into an exam answer.
Students are told to use AI as a supplement, preserve their own thinking, and critically verify its output.

kp.k: Submitted-work rules protect independent legal analysis and authorship
kp.d: The submitted-work topic covers 94 schools and records materially different boundaries, rather than a uniform ban. Stanford requires written authorization for substantive drafting, revision or paraphrasing; Columbia permits testing arguments and improving expression but bars outsourcing assessed legal analysis. Berkeley's default extends to conceptualizing and outlining, while Hofstra's no-guidance rule emphasizes citation, critical evaluation and responsibility. Several records separately distinguish ordinary grammar or source-finding tools from substantive generation.
qs: Generative AI may not draft, revise, or paraphrase substantive submitted work unless the instructor gives written authorization.
It may not perform the legal analysis an assignment assesses or generate work submitted for academic credit, and any AI contribution to submitted work must be disclosed.
The policy prohibits AI aid in conceptualizing, outlining, drafting, revising, translating, or editing work submitted for credit; research use is limited to identifying sources.
Submitted assignments must follow the instructor's AI rules; when no guidance is provided, students must cite AI-derived content, evaluate it critically, and remain responsible for the final work.

kp.k: Exam restrictions distinguish preparation from live AI assistance
kp.d: The exam topic contains 67 schools. Numerous summaries describe default prohibitions with instructor-authorized exceptions, including for open-internet exams. Rules also differ over pre-generated material: Case Western permits reliance on AI material prepared before an exam under its default, whereas Berkeley prohibits an AI-generated outline when its elements are used on the exam. These distinctions preclude treating study permission as exam permission.
qs: Even on an open-book or open-internet exam, generative AI is unauthorized unless the exam instructions expressly permit it.
Students may rely on AI-generated material prepared before an exam, but may not prompt AI or use information from another person's exam-time prompt during the exam.
AI use is prohibited for any purpose in an exam situation; the policy treats an AI-generated exam outline as prohibited when its elements are used on the exam.

kp.k: Schools are redesigning assessments to preserve independent performance
kp.d: The archive reports Texas's near-elimination of take-home exams and increased secure in-class and live assessment. UC Law San Francisco began implementing a presumption of in-person, closed-book exams in 2023–24. For 2026–27, Chicago reports a coordinated first-year no-access exam pilot, while Suffolk's interim measures require secure software for specified foundational summative assessments, subject to exceptions and alternatives. These are reported strategies, not evidence of measured effectiveness.
qs: The school reports near-elimination of take-home exams, a sharp increase in secure in-class exams, and a surge of interest in class-participation and live-presentation assessments, including oral exams in some cases.

Under its adopted Supplemental Strategic Plan on Generative AI, UC Law SF shifted to a presumption of in-person, closed-book exams to address assessment integrity; implementation began during the 2023–24 academic year.
For 2026–27, the school is piloting coordinated in-class, no-access exam conditions across required first-year courses.

For 2026–27, the memo sets an interim requirement that summative assessments in specified foundational courses use secure software that blocks internet and local-file access, subject to accommodations, other authorized exceptions, and dean-approved alternatives.

kp.k: Course-rule transparency accompanies decentralized AI permissions
kp.d: The 64-school course-disclosure topic distinguishes instructor communication from students' attribution of AI use. Approaches range from nonbinding syllabus models and written notice of deviations to requirements for every course. Syracuse mandates selection of exactly one of three prescribed statements; Wisconsin requires a communicated syllabus policy and retains a prohibition if none is supplied. Belmont additionally requires disclosure of faculty AI use for grading assistance or feedback.
qs: Student attribution or disclosure of AI use, standing alone, does not qualify.
Every course must reproduce the University's required language and select exactly one of three prescribed AI statements; instructors may not substitute their own statement.
Every faculty member must establish and clearly communicate a course AI policy and include it in the syllabus and, when appropriate, Canvas.
Faculty must also disclose in the syllabus any use of AI for grading assistance or student feedback.

kp.k: Upload restrictions protect instructional content and student privacy
kp.d: Uploading materials is the smallest topic, with 13 schools, not evidence that other schools lack protections. Records address faculty intellectual property, class recordings, peer contributions and FERPA-protected work. Berkeley broadly prohibits uploading class content; Stetson permits specified protected inputs only with written student consent or an expressly approved institutional tool. Suffolk's 2026–27 interim restriction requires instructor and affected-student permission and expires June 30, 2027 unless extended or replaced. CUNY and Syracuse destination-neutral restrictions are explicitly interpreted as encompassing AI platforms.
qs: Students may not upload assignments, readings, slides, recordings, or other class content to generative AI systems.

Stetson tells faculty not to use FERPA-protected student work—including grades, graded work, and ungraded assignments—as input to a generative-AI tool without the student's written consent, unless the tool is Stetson-provided and expressly approved for FERPA-protected inputs; students are also cautioned to respect copyright restrictions.
The measure expires June 30, 2027, unless extended or replaced.
Because the rule is destination-neutral, it encompasses AI platforms.

kp.k: Mandatory AI literacy takes multiple curricular forms
kp.d: The archive includes 31 schools under mandatory curriculum, spanning orientation, embedded legal-research-and-writing instruction, certifications, stand-alone courses and multi-year training. Inclusion does not mean 31 currently operative requirements: Lewis & Clark and New York Law School are Proposed, and some cohort offerings are Completed/limited. Albany's required one-credit first-year program begins with the 2026–27 entering class; UC Law San Francisco's six-session second-year lab becomes mandatory for the Class of 2029 and awards a certificate rather than academic credit.
qs: AI instruction required for all students, a defined entering cohort, or a degree-program cohort.
Beginning with the incoming 2026–27 class, all first-year students will take the required, one-credit Introduction to Law Practice in the Digital Age.
Implementation is underway, but the source does not establish that the requirement is yet operative.
Starting with the incoming Class of 2029, every J.D. student will be required to complete the six-session AI-Enabled Lawyering Lab during the second year.
The professional-development program awards a certificate of completion rather than academic credit.

kp.k: Foundational competence is paired with supervised AI practice
kp.d: Several curricular records explicitly preserve unaided analytical skills alongside AI training. Penn introduces structured AI lessons after foundational analysis and writing; Chicago's Autumn 2026 first-year pilot combines device-free classrooms with unaided and supervised AI-assisted legal research and writing. Boston College's required sequence includes a graded exercise verifying, critiquing and revising AI-assisted work. Texas identifies de-skilling risks without announcing a single schoolwide coursework rule.
qs: The required first-year Legal Practice Skills sequence uses a structured series of AI lessons and exercises after students establish foundational analytical and writing skills.

The 2026–27 pilot pairs device-free classrooms across all core 1L sections with a layered legal-research-and-writing approach that teaches students to work both without AI and with supervised AI assistance.

The required first-year Law Practice sequence continues AI training with CoCounsel and Protégé, followed by a graded assignment in which students verify, critique, and revise AI-assisted work as the curriculum evolves.
The strategy identifies productive study uses and de-skilling risks but does not announce one school-wide rule for AI use in coursework.

kp.k: AI governance education differs from practice-tool instruction
kp.d: The archive separates optional law-of-AI instruction, cataloged at 70 schools, from practice-focused tech-of-law instruction at 50. The former addresses AI-specific regulation, rights, duties and liability; the latter addresses legal work and professional tool use. One qualifying course suffices, and schools can appear in both. Counts encompass scheduled, maintained and qualifying prior-year offerings, not necessarily recurring current classes or comprehensive programs; platform access alone and non-J.D. offerings do not qualify.
qs: Law of AI covers instruction primarily about legal doctrine, regulation, policy, governance, rights, duties, or liability evolving in response to AI.
Tech of law covers instruction primarily about AI's effect on legal work or how lawyers use AI.
A school may appear in both tabs when its instruction substantially satisfies both definitions.
Platform access without instruction, non-J.D. offerings, older past-only activities, and merely planned offerings without a start term are excluded.

kp.k: Practice instruction targets workflows, tool-building and professional judgment
kp.d: The practice-focused records describe training for research, drafting, discovery, contract analysis, advocacy and workflow design, alongside prompting, verification, confidentiality and human judgment. Berkeley's Fall 2026 three-credit elective promises more than 100 hours of hands-on training for 2Ls and 3Ls. Virginia's lab has students build workflow-automation tools, while Delaware's Fall 2026 curriculum includes agentic research and law-firm management. These are educational offerings, not measured productivity or employment effects.
qs: Beginning Fall 2026, the three-credit AI and the Practice of Law: Public Interest & Private Practice course gives 2L and 3L students more than 100 hours of hands-on training in AI-assisted legal work while emphasizing judgment, quality, and responsible use.
For Fall 2026, Virginia offers AI and Legal Tools Lab, where students identify legal workflows suitable for AI augmentation and build tools to automate those tasks.
AI-Empowered Lawyering covers prompt engineering, agentic research, AI-assisted writing, e-discovery, predictive analytics, law-firm management, and related ethical and evidentiary issues.

kp.k: Vendor partnerships provide tools and structured educational support
kp.d: The archive reports legal-AI and training-provider involvement in student and faculty formation. Penn State Dickinson's Harvey partnership supports study uses and training; Notre Dame's supervised Harvey deployment in two Advanced Legal Research courses is specifically limited to Spring 2025 evidence. Santa Clara integrates a six-class Hotshot curriculum into a required first-year course. Northwestern's Legal AI Scholars Program provides practical and ethical AI-assisted lawyering training. The records do not establish comparative vendor efficacy.
qs: Through the law school's Harvey partnership, students can use the platform to summarize notes and other materials, create outlines and study guides, and generate retrieval-practice questions, while remaining responsible for verifying the output.
Completed in Spring 2025: Notre Dame expanded its Harvey pilot to two Advanced Legal Research courses, where students used the platform under supervision.
The public source does not establish continued course deployment after that term.
A six-class generative-AI curriculum covering legal applications, prompting, ethics, and professional responsibility is mandatory in the first-year Critical Lawyering Skills course.
Northwestern's Legal AI Scholars Program provides practical and ethical AI-assisted lawyering training.

kp.k: Experiential AI programs address unmet legal needs
kp.d: Some optional programs expressly connect technical training with access to justice. Duke's Fall 2026 practicum involves auditing, testing and red-teaming legal-service AI with courts, legal-aid organizations and nonprofits. Penn's year-long Fall 2026 lab includes AI legal assistance and document automation intended to expand access to justice. ASU offers applied community-needs pathways, while Hofstra fellows are developing an AI disability-benefits eligibility application. These are program activities and objectives, not demonstrated reductions in unmet need.
qs: In the Fall 2026 AI Audits Practicum, J.D. students work with courts, legal-aid organizations, and nonprofits to audit, test, and red-team AI products used to provide legal services.

For Fall 2026, Penn Carey Law offers the year-long Legal Access and Innovation Lab ('Legal AI Lab'), in which students design, build, and evaluate tools—including AI-driven legal assistance and document automation—to expand access to justice while developing skills for technology-enabled research, drafting, and client service.
Beginning Fall 2026, students in the AI and Legal Tech Studio follow applied pathways in building AI-enabled legal applications or using AI to address access-to-justice and community needs.

The Deans' Legal-Tech Fellowship brings law and computer-science students together to build legal-technology tools; fellows are currently developing an AI application that determines eligibility for Social Security disability benefits.

kp.k: Faculty support extends beyond permission-setting to teaching redesign
kp.d: The faculty-support topic includes 93 schools and spans law-library guides, consultations, workshops, committees and curriculum coordination, including universitywide resources and completed training. Georgetown offers customized pedagogical support and classroom or clinic guest lectures; LSU's faculty sandbox supports preparation, exam writing and curriculum development. Suffolk encourages pilots of oral defenses or AI-use documentation for substantial papers. Inclusion does not imply a continuing school-specific training program in every case.
qs: Courses offered to students and mere instructor discretion to set a course rule do not qualify on their own.

Georgetown Law's faculty AI resources include consultations, workshops, customized pedagogical support, a teaching guide for integrating AI and designing assignments and policies, and law-library guest lectures for classes and clinics.
The Law Profs' AI Sandbox offers legal educators tutorials and tailored guidance for class preparation, exam writing, curriculum development, course policies, and responsible AI use.

The 2026–27 interim measures also encourage faculty supervising substantial papers to pilot oral defenses or AI-use documentation, while the Teaching Committee will gather and share effective practices and recommend faculty training and support, disclosure norms, and human-review standards.

kp.k: AI detection raises evidentiary and privacy concerns
kp.d: The Louisville record cautions that uploading student work to third-party detectors can create privacy, FERPA and consent risks, notes the absence of an institutional detector contract, and rejects detector output as the sole basis for an integrity decision. Other faculty-support records include detector limitations and responses to suspected misuse. These are institutional cautions, not quantified findings about detector accuracy.
qs: UofL cautions that third-party AI detectors often require student work to be uploaded to unvetted platforms, creating privacy, FERPA, and consent risks.
UofL has no institutional AI-detector contract, and detector output should not be the sole basis for an integrity decision.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Perlman's archive describes differentiated institutional adaptation to AI in legal education, rather than predicting a uniform transformation of legal markets.
pts.d: The principal claim is descriptive: public records from 163 U.S. law schools document changes to student-use rules, assessment, curriculum, and faculty support. The workbook contains 524 overlapping school-topic records: studying and learning 42; submitted work 94; exams 67; course-policy disclosure 64; uploading materials 13; mandatory curriculum 31; optional law-of-AI instruction 70; optional practice-focused instruction 50; faculty support 93. These are counts of catalogued coverage, not counts of schools implementing one common policy. Perlman expressly disclaims endorsement or ranking. The source offers no quantified forecast of lawyer displacement, legal-service prices, or market restructuring.

pts.k: AI is being accommodated as a study aid while many catalogued policies preserve independent analysis and restrict AI-produced assessed work.
pts.d: Perlman's introductory synthesis says the catalogued study approaches generally permit limited assistance with independent judgment and accuracy checks. School summaries identify explanations, outlines, practice questions, brainstorming, and research leads as possible uses; these permissions are not findings that learning outcomes improve. The archive describes a distinction between augmentation of learning and substitution for the student's own legal analysis. For example, its Columbia entry permits argument testing and language assistance but bars AI from performing the analysis being assessed. Its Texas strategy summary acknowledges productive study uses alongside de-skilling risks, without quantifying either.

pts.k: The archive reports that AI is prompting changes in how schools establish assessment integrity, including secure examinations and live assessments.
pts.d: These are school-specific institutional reports reproduced in Perlman's summaries, not a quantified national trend. Texas reports a near-elimination of take-home examinations and increased secure in-class and live assessment. UC Law San Francisco reports a presumption of in-person, closed-book exams beginning in 2023–24. Chicago's 2026–27 pilot coordinates no-access first-year examinations; Suffolk's interim measures require secure software for specified foundational-course summative assessments, with exceptions. The source does not measure the effectiveness of these changes.

pts.k: Legal education is adding AI literacy, supervised tool use, verification, and professional judgment to required and optional instruction.
pts.d: The archive describes mandatory orientation sessions, integrated first-year research-and-writing instruction, certificates, and multiyear training, alongside adopted future requirements and proposals. Its Boston College summary describes a graded exercise requiring verification, critique, and revision of AI-assisted work. Penn Carey introduces structured AI exercises after foundational skills are established. Optional offerings teach research, drafting, contract review, workflow design, and tool development. Separately, law-of-AI offerings address regulation, governance, rights, and liability; these are not interchangeable with practice-skills instruction. Course descriptions establish educational content and aims, not demonstrated professional productivity or competence gains.

pts.k: Practice-focused program descriptions present AI as supporting or automating legal workflows and as a possible means of expanding legal assistance.
pts.d: Perlman's summaries attribute these propositions to institutional programs rather than establishing them through measured service outcomes. Dayton's microcredential teaches that AI can streamline research and writing; Virginia's lab identifies workflows suitable for augmentation and builds automation tools. Penn Carey's Legal Access and Innovation Lab aims to expand access to justice through AI assistance and document automation. Duke's practicum involves auditing, testing, and red-teaming AI products used in legal services. These examples support claims about training activities and intended applications; the archive does not report achieved time savings, automation rates, or reductions in unmet legal need.

pts.k: AI is generating new faculty-support activities, course-communication duties, and constraints on sharing educational materials.
pts.d: The archive documents workshops, resource guides, curricular committees, and assistance with AI-informed assignment and assessment design. Some schools require every course to disclose its AI rules; others only recommend disclosure or require notice of departures from defaults. Upload policies address confidentiality, intellectual property, student contributions, and education records. These measures concern students and faculty, including faculty use of AI for feedback or grading. Availability of universitywide support is distinguished from a law-school-specific program, and the archive does not establish actual participation rates.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is a source-linked documentary inventory, substantially researched and summarized with AI, not an outcome study or a comprehensive adoption survey.
pts.d: Sources include handbooks, honor codes, university policies, library guidance, official course catalogs and schedules, institutional announcements, and strategy memoranda. The roster was cross-checked against the ABA Council's approved-school list. The archive distinguishes binding policies, nonbinding guidance, and institutional support, and supplies status labels and source links. Perlman discloses that he has not personally reviewed or independently confirmed every reference or summary. The document reports source-to-summary checks as of August 8, 2026, while acknowledging remaining errors and omissions. The appended derived tabulations are arithmetic over the captured workbook, explicitly not claims made by the archive itself. No learning-outcome experiment, legal-work benchmark, or labor-market dataset substantiates the educational and professional benefits described here.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source is an August 2026 snapshot mixing operative measures, prior offerings, future commitments, pilots, and proposals; implementation cannot be inferred from inclusion alone.
pts.d: Research was last updated August 8, 2026; the site was captured August 11 and re-fetched August 13, when the workbook was also captured. Examples include Columbia's August 1, 2026 policy; Washington's September 30, 2026 changes; Albany's incoming 2026–27 requirement; and UC Law SF's requirement for the Class of 2029 during its second year, while the lab remains voluntary for 2026–27 upper-level students. Lewis & Clark's mandatory-literacy plan and NYLS's first-year integration remain unconfirmed as operative in the summaries. Optional-instruction inclusion can rest on a maintained listing, a future schedule, or a prior-year course, not necessarily a currently running class. Narrative dates and qualifications matter even where entries carry an 'In effect' label. Course-specific permission, verification, confidentiality, and accommodation provisions condition many student-use rules.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate affected groups are J.D. students, faculty, librarians, and law-school administrators; downstream effects on lawyers, clients, and the public are principally educational aims.
pts.d: Students encounter new permissions and prohibitions, disclosure and verification responsibilities, assessment formats, and AI-literacy requirements that may differ by course or entering cohort. Faculty must or are encouraged to communicate boundaries, redesign teaching and assessments, protect student records, and develop AI skills; libraries, technology staff, and committees provide support. Future lawyers are trained for AI-assisted research, drafting, analysis, and service delivery. Courts, legal-aid organizations, nonprofits, and people with unmet legal needs feature in applied programs, but the archive does not establish realized effects on those beneficiaries. The inventory focuses on enrolled J.D. education and excludes standalone CLE, executive education, LL.M.-only, and other non-J.D. optional offerings. It provides no basis for differential employment forecasts by firm size, seniority, or provider type.
